actions.visual_identity_evidence: Opposite viewing directions place these similar landscapes on separate end walls: one beside the bookcase, the other beside the hallway door. Their approximately 5.3-unit separation supports this structural distinction; shot2 excludes furniture handling, and neither frames nor story support remounting the painting.

The narrow corner table at the bookcase end and wider drawer console beside the opposite doorway belong to different wall installations. Approximately 4.2-unit separation and differing widths corroborate the images; relocation would require the unsupported furniture rearrangement explicitly excluded by shot2.

Independent review finds generic round leaves on different supports, with much fuller trailing growth in shot3 and approximately 4-unit center separation. Separate plants are plausible, but shot1 detail cannot rule out relocation or appearance drift; shot2 authorizes no such move, so common identity remains unresolved.

Similar landscape motifs repeat on opposite end walls: shot1 faces the bookcase end, shot3 the hallway end. The 5.29-unit separation supports this structural distinction; camera reversal cannot move a wall mounting. Relocation is unsupported visually and conflicts with shot2's no-rearrangement fact.

Shot1's narrow single-drawer table and shot3's broad two-knob console occupy opposite window ends, established by bookcase versus doorway context. The 4.23-unit separation corroborates different supports; neither perspective nor relocation explains both structure and placement, and shot2 prohibits furniture movement.

Independently of the rejected support match, shot1 shows a compact crown with sparse trailing growth, while shot3 has a broad crown and multiple long cascades at the opposite room end. Their 3.99-unit separation agrees with distinct planted arrangements; relocation plus major foliage change lacks visual support and conflicts with shot2's no-rearrangement fact.

Repeated landscape imagery does not overcome wall identity: A is on the bookcase end wall, B above the console on the opposite end wall under the reverse view. Relocation would require an unshown wall transfer despite shot2's unchanged-room fact; this is structural context, not an inferred box displacement.

A's narrow corner stand and B's broad drawer console occupy opposite end-wall contexts relative to the common window and desk. Foreshortening alone is insufficient; a furniture transfer conflicts with shot2's no-movement fact, and no aligned extents were supplied to override or corroborate the images.

Independently of the rejected supports, A has a small sparse crown and thin rightward trail, while B has a fuller crown and long left cascade at the opposite wall. Distinct stable placements plus shot2's unchanged-room fact favor separate plants over an unshown transfer; leaf similarity alone is insufficient.
